title: The Solution to the Power Grid's Woes Might Just Be Sitting in Your Driveway
gist: A coalition of Eversource, National Grid, EnergyHub, Sunrun, and the Mobility House is launching a Massachusetts pilot for vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology, letting EV owners get paid to discharge their batteries back into the grid during peak demand, positioning V2G as a cheap alternative to new storage and transmission buildout.

insights.claim: Eversource, National Grid, EnergyHub, Sunrun, and the Mobility House launched an early vehicle-to-grid (V2G) test in Massachusetts, letting utility customers try discharging their EV batteries back into the grid via the existing ConnectedSolutions demand-response program.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Watch this multi-utility, multi-vendor coalition pilot as the reference case other US utilities will copy or license lessons from when scaling V2G programs.
insights.locator: You can’t tell when you’re passing one on the highway

insights.claim: Sunrun's director of grid services, Chip Silverman, said Massachusetts taking an early-mover role on V2G will generate the operational learnings needed to scale the technology more broadly.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Massachusetts pilot outcomes are a leading indicator for how fast V2G programs replicate in other states.
insights.quote: It’s great to have Massachusetts stepping into the lead here and doing this because these learnings are what’s going to allow this technology to scale
insights.locator: Utilities across the country are pursuing pilot projects

insights.claim: In the Massachusetts pilot, participants use an app to specify when they typically need their vehicle (e.g., commuting hours), letting utilities coordinate discharge timing without disrupting owners' driving schedules.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Scheduling apps are the coordination layer that determines whether V2G programs can scale to fleets without user friction.
insights.locator: These early projects are figuring out how best to coordinate this

insights.claim: US electricity demand is rising simultaneously from power-hungry data centers coming online, drivers switching from gas cars to EVs, and homeowners switching from gas furnaces to heat pumps, while utilities are also trying to replace gas and coal with intermittent renewables like wind and solar.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Compounding demand growth plus renewable intermittency is the structural driver behind utility interest in flexible storage like V2G and grid battery buildout.
insights.locator: Utilities like V2G because they’re dealing with escalating

insights.claim: US electricity prices are already rising due to utility shareholder profits and customers footing the bill for infrastructure upgrades like burying power lines to prevent wildfire and storm damage, with more battery and transmission buildout set to add further costs.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Rising baseline electricity costs from grid-hardening capex create the affordability pressure that makes cheaper alternatives like V2G commercially attractive to regulators and utilities.
insights.locator: Already, Americans are struggling with skyrocketing energy prices

insights.claim: A hotter climate creates a self-reinforcing demand loop: more heat drives more air-conditioning use, which increases electricity demand, and if that power isn't renewable it adds more warming emissions, further increasing AC demand.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: This feedback loop raises the stakes for pairing flexible resources like V2G with renewable generation rather than fossil peaker plants during heat-driven demand spikes.
insights.locator: The hotter the planet gets, the more enticing V2G looks

themes.theme: V2G as Cheap Alternative to New Storage

insights.claim: EV owners with vehicle-to-grid capability are compensated by utilities to discharge their batteries into the grid only during a small number of hours per year, during specific demand-response events, not on a daily basis.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Low-frequency discharge cycles minimize battery degradation concerns for EV owners considering enrolling in V2G programs, removing a key adoption objection.
insights.quote: It’s really kind of a small number of hours per year that you’re discharging the battery
insights.locator: In the new system, participants hook into an existing program

insights.claim: The Mobility House's Russell Vare argues V2G is the cheapest source of flexible energy storage utilities can currently access, because it taps existing, already-purchased EV batteries rather than requiring utilities to build new storage infrastructure from scratch.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: If V2G undercuts new battery-storage buildout costs, utilities and regulators have a direct financial incentive to fund bidirectional-charger incentive programs instead of new grid-scale storage capex.
insights.quote: It’s the cheapest cost of flexible energy storage that will be available for the grid
insights.locator: Except some of that spending may indeed be avoidable

insights.claim: A typical EV battery has roughly six times the storage capacity of a home backup battery unit mounted outside a house, making it a far larger reserve of grid-usable energy per vehicle.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: The capacity gap versus dedicated home batteries explains why utilities see EV fleets, not standalone home storage, as the more capital-efficient flexible-resource play.
insights.locator: Even a typical EV battery, though, has around six times

insights.claim: Sunrun's Chip Silverman said that aggregating a larger number of EV batteries into a virtual power plant lets each individual battery contribute less energy while the pooled resource still becomes very large collectively.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Program design should prioritize maximizing enrolled-vehicle count over per-vehicle discharge depth, since aggregation scale is what unlocks grid-relevant capacity with minimal wear per battery.
insights.quote: If you have a higher number of batteries out there in a virtual power plant, you can actually use less energy from each individual battery. But collectively, when you patch them all together and aggregate them, it comes out to a very large resource. And that’s really where the magic is.
insights.locator: With EVs sitting idle all across a city

insights.claim: Only a fraction of EV owners in a given area would need to enroll in V2G for a program to adequately support the grid, though more participants improves the resource base a utility can draw from.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Utilities don't need mass EV adoption to make V2G viable, lowering the bar for near-term program impact even in markets with modest EV penetration.
insights.locator: With EVs sitting idle all across a city

insights.claim: Vehicles that follow predictable schedules, like school buses and municipal fleets, are especially valuable for V2G because their usage patterns are easy to plan around and their batteries are typically large.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Fleet operators (school districts, municipalities) are a near-term target segment for V2G deployment ahead of broad consumer adoption, given predictable idle time and large battery packs.
insights.locator: In a V2G system, vehicles that follow predictable schedules

insights.claim: More EV models, including the Nissan Leaf, are shipping with the hardware needed to support vehicle-to-grid discharge, though not all EVs currently have this capability.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: V2G-ready EV model availability is a gating factor for program growth; track OEM rollout of bidirectional-capable models as an adoption signal.
insights.locator: While not all EVs have the hardware needed to tap into V2G

insights.claim: EnergyHub president Seth Frader-Thompson predicts vehicle-to-grid will become dramatically more accessible over the next several years as bidirectional-charger hardware costs fall, installation gets simpler, and industry standards mature.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Falling bidirectional-charger costs and standards maturation are the catalysts to watch for a V2G inflection point in mainstream EV ownership.
insights.quote: As hardware costs come down, installation becomes simpler, and standards continue to mature, we expect vehicle-to-grid to become dramatically more accessible over the next several years
insights.locator: While not all EVs have the hardware needed to tap into V2G

insights.claim: V2G discharge is designed to happen when grid demand peaks, such as when people return home from work and switch on appliances, with vehicles then recharging overnight using active managed charging that staggers charge start times so EVs aren't all drawing power simultaneously at a single peak hour like 10pm.
insights.speaker: Matt Simon
insights.so_what: Active managed charging is the complementary control layer that prevents mass EV charging from creating new demand spikes even as V2G smooths existing ones.
insights.locator: The overall idea is for EVs to send power back to the grid
